title: A Tiny Robot That Swims With Living Muscle
summary:
Scientists at MIT have built a tiny robot that swims with real, living muscle instead of batteries and motors.

The robot's body is soft and flexible, about the size of a stick of gum. It has two fins, and each fin is covered with muscle cells much thinner than a human hair. Scientists changed the cells so they squeeze tight when light shines on them. By flashing light on one fin or the other, the team can steer the robot and change its speed.

In tests, the robot swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At its fastest, it moved about four body lengths every minute. An Olympic swimmer can move up to 65 body lengths a minute.

Study author Ritu Raman said it takes a lot of force to move through water, and the robot is quite strong for its size. The study appeared in the journal Advanced Functional Materials. One day, robots like this might do gentle jobs in fragile places, because living tissue is soft and can even heal itself.
why_it_matters: One day, soft robots like this could explore fragile places you care about, like coral reefs, without damaging them.

background_read: Most robots move with motors and batteries, but some scientists are building a new kind of robot that uses living parts, like real muscle.
Muscle works by squeezing tight and then relaxing, and that squeezing can push a robot through the water.
Scientists like these soft, living robots because tissue is gentle and can even heal itself after it is hurt.
